newsitem.title: USA: US DOE mulls opening of public utility power lines.
newsitem.headline: US DOE mulls opening of public utility power lines.

text.p: The Clinton administration is considering asking Congress to give the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC) authority to require public utilities to open their transmission lines to other power producers, an Energy Department official said Tuesday.

Currently, under its open access rules in Order 888, the commission may only require a public utility, such as a municipally-owned facility, to open its transmission lines to others if the public utility wants access to investor-owned utilities' lines.
The question is "should Order 888 be extended to non-jurisdictional facilities, which we're considering," said Doug Smith, the Energy Department's deputy general counsel for energy policy.
Order 888 required all investor-owned utilities to open their transmission lines to competing power producers selling electricity for resale.

The Energy Department is close to completing its proposals for legislation on opening all power markets to competition, and the draft must now be reviewed by other agencies, Smith said at a National Association of Manufacturers conference.

Unlike legislation introduced in the House and Senate which set deadlines on states ranging from the end of 2000 to 2003, Energy Department officials have repeatedly said they do not favor imposing a deadline on states to give all consumers freedom to choose their electricity suppliers.

Smith said the Energy Department is leaning in favor of proposing a federal public benefits fund with a small fee on electricity as it enters the power grid, to be used to match state funding of programs such as guaranteeing service to low-income homes and protecting the environment.
The administration is also still considering calling for a renewable energy standard that would guarantee some marketshare for electricity produced from renewable fuels.

Smith said the main questions were what percentage of power should be produced from renewables and whether hydropower should be included, as it was in a bill by Sen. Dale Bumpers, a Democrat from Arkansas.

He said if the main purpose of the protection for renewables was to encourage the building of new capacity, hydropower should not be included, since it is a mature technology that would continue to run cheaply without any incentives.
"The purpose of having a renewables policy ... is to get new capacity on line," he said.
Smith declined to say whether the administration would support the sweeping electric restructuring bill reintroduced Monday by Republican Rep. Dan Schaefer of Colorado.
"The (Energy) Department doesn't have a formal position on that," he said.
